title: Herter Brothers Secretary from the Jay Gould House (1882)
summary: A drop-front secretary made by Herter Brothers in 1882 for railroad financier Jay Gould's New York house, with a dark ebonized case framing bands of light, pictorial marquetry.
description: Herter Brothers was the most fashionable decorating firm in Gilded Age New York, and this secretary shows why. The case is ebonized cherry, a near-black finish that makes the inlaid panels of lighter wood read like framed pictures. Each drawer front carries its own band of marquetry, and the fall front is treated as a single centerpiece panel. The Aesthetic Movement liked exactly this contrast: a calm, rectilinear box carrying very fine surface decoration. For cabinetry today, the lesson is proportion and contrast. Keep the carcass simple and dark, and let a small number of richly figured or inlaid fronts do the talking. The same approach works on a library wall, a bar cabinet, or a run of drawer fronts in a dressing room.
makeItToday: Ebonized maple or cherry fronts with CNC-cut inlay pockets filled with contrasting veneer; a Signature version can use laser-cut veneer appliqué instead of true marquetry.
medium: Ebonized cherry, mahogany, cedar, and brass

title: Herter Brothers Painted and Gilded Display Cabinet (c. 1883)
summary: A Herter Brothers maple cabinet from about 1883 with a painted and gilded finish, bevelled glass doors and open display shelves set into an architectural, pagoda-like frame.
description: This cabinet mixes closed storage, glazed doors and open shelving in one composition, which is why it is useful to anyone planning a display wall or china cabinet. Herter Brothers built it in maple, then painted and gilded the surface and lined the interior with silk velvet so collected objects would glow against a deep ground. The upper section steps back like a small building, with slender turned supports and a shaped cornice; the lower doors are flat panels with delicate gilt borders. It is a good example of how late-Victorian makers layered materials rather than relying on heavy carving. A modern version could keep the stepped silhouette and contrasting interior color while using a durable painted finish and LED-lit shelves.
makeItToday: Paint-grade maple or poplar frame, CNC-shaped cornice and brackets, glass-panel doors and a painted or fabric-lined interior; gilding can be replaced with metallic paint or leaf on the moulding edges.
medium: Maple, with painted and gilded surface, bevelled glass, silk velvet, brass

title: Herter Brothers Wardrobe with Inlaid Panels (1875–1883)
summary: A tall two-door cherry wardrobe by Herter Brothers with a dark finish, inset door panels scattered with small inlaid flowers and a band of ornament at the cornice.
description: Before built-in closets were common, a wardrobe like this held a household's clothing, and its design translates directly to a modern closet wall or bedroom built-in. The doors are framed with narrow stiles and rails, and each recessed panel is scattered with small floral inlays rather than covered edge to edge, which keeps a large surface from feeling busy. A decorative frieze across the top and a matching band across the base tie the piece together. Herter Brothers often used this restrained Anglo-Japanese approach in bedrooms. For a built-in wardrobe today, the same idea works: a quiet dark or painted frame, one repeated motif, and a defined top and bottom band.
makeItToday: Stile-and-rail doors with CNC-routed recessed panels; the scattered motif can be V-carved and color-filled or applied as inlaid veneer roundels.

title: Kimbel and Cabus Modern Gothic Hanging Key Cabinet (c. 1874)
summary: An oak hanging key cabinet made around 1874 by the New York firm Kimbel and Cabus in the Modern Gothic style, with pointed cresting, chamfered edges and pierced metal strapwork on the door.
description: Kimbel and Cabus were leaders of the American Modern Gothic style, which borrowed the spires, chamfers and strap hinges of medieval furniture and simplified them for machine production. This small cabinet hung on a wall to hold household keys. Its silhouette rises to pointed finials, the frame is chamfered and incised, and the single door carries decorative metal strapwork over a plain oak panel. Pieces like this show how much character a tiny wall cabinet can carry. Similar proportions work for a medicine cabinet, a spice cabinet in a period kitchen, or a mudroom key box beside the back door.
makeItToday: Quarter-sawn oak with CNC-cut cresting and chamfers; the strapwork can be laser-cut steel or brass, or V-carved as a surface pattern.

title: Charles Tisch Inlaid Rosewood Cabinet (c. 1884)
summary: A New York cabinet by Charles Tisch from about 1884, built in rosewood and inlaid with ivory, mother-of-pearl and other woods, combining glazed cases, open shelves and turned spindles.
description: Charles Tisch worked in the same lavish Aesthetic Movement circle as Herter Brothers, and this cabinet is a catalog of the period's favorite devices. It combines a mirrored upper stage, glazed side cases, spindle galleries, open shelves and inlaid panels in a single, asymmetrical composition. The dark rosewood ground makes the light inlay stand out sharply. Few modern homes need a piece this elaborate, but its parts are useful: spindle galleries for open shelving, asymmetric glazed and solid doors, and a contrasting inlay band. A bar or butler's pantry is a natural place to borrow from it.
makeItToday: Heirloom-tier work: dark-stained walnut or rosewood veneer, CNC-turned spindles, and inlay pockets machined for contrasting veneer or shell-look laminate.

title: Herter Brothers Oak Sideboard with Foliate Panels (1876–80)
summary: A tall carved oak sideboard by Herter Brothers with foliate panels, small Romanesque arches and turned, chamfered details, made in New York in the late 1870s.
description: A dining room sideboard of this scale was effectively a built-in: it stood over seven feet tall and anchored the room. Herter Brothers carved its oak doors with stylized leaves, set small arches into the upper gallery, and used turned and chamfered posts to give it a vertical rhythm. The base offers deep cupboards and drawers; the upper tiers display plates and silver. Today the same layout makes an excellent built-in buffet or butler's pantry wall: closed storage below a counter, shallow open display above, and carved panels used only on the doors where they will be seen at eye level.

title: Daniel Pabst Modern Gothic Sideboard (1868–80)
summary: A walnut and burled-elm sideboard from Daniel Pabst's Philadelphia workshop, carved in the Modern Gothic style associated with architect Frank Furness.
description: Daniel Pabst was Philadelphia's leading cabinetmaker of the 1870s and often collaborated with the architect Frank Furness. This sideboard shows their bold Modern Gothic vocabulary: crisp, stylized carving, chamfered edges, a crested top and panels of figured burl set into walnut. The carving is flat and graphic rather than naturalistic, which makes it well suited to machine production today. A three-door base with drawers and a tall shelved back is also a sensible layout for a built-in dining hutch.
makeItToday: Walnut frame with burl veneer panels and 2.5D CNC relief carving; the graphic Furness-style motifs translate cleanly to V-carved and pocketed toolpaths.

title: William Burges Painted Sideboard and Wine Cabinet (1859)
summary: A Gothic Revival sideboard and wine cabinet designed by architect William Burges in 1859, painted and gilded with figurative scenes and tracery inspired by medieval cathedrals and manuscripts.
description: William Burges treated furniture as architecture. This piece, made by Harland & Fisher, uses painted pine and mahogany as a canvas for scenes and patterns drawn from Gothic tracery, stained glass and illuminated manuscripts. The structure itself is simple: a deep cabinet on short legs with a stepped, arcaded front. Its impact comes from color and painted narrative. That makes it a useful reference for anyone who wants a bold statement piece without complex joinery. A painted island end, bar front or built-in cabinet could borrow its palette and arcading.

summary: A walnut drawing room cabinet designed by Bruce James Talbert and made by Gillow & Co. in Lancaster, England, combining Gothic structure with inlaid panels of ebony, boxwood and thuya.
description: Bruce Talbert was one of the most influential furniture designers of Victorian Britain, and his book Gothic Forms Applied to Furniture shaped the work of American makers too. This cabinet shows his approach: a rectilinear frame with visible structure, turned colonnettes, and flat panels decorated with inlay rather than deep carving. The center is open beneath a writing surface, flanked by cupboards with geometric inlaid doors. The design suits a home office built-in or a library wall where storage, a desk and display share one composition.

title: E. W. Godwin Anglo-Japanese Sideboard (designed 1867)
summary: An ebonized mahogany sideboard designed by Edward William Godwin in 1867 and made by William Watt around 1876, a landmark of the Anglo-Japanese style.
description: Godwin's sideboard looks surprisingly modern for the 1860s. Inspired by Japanese architecture, he reduced the piece to a black rectilinear frame of thin members, open shelves and a few closed cupboards with simple brass fittings and leaded glass. The empty spaces matter as much as the solid ones. This is a valuable reference for clean-lined cabinetry that still feels historic: open shelving supported by visible frames, flat slab doors, and a single dark finish. It sits comfortably next to contemporary interiors.

title: George Croome Renaissance Revival Cabinet, Boston (1875–77)
summary: A mahogany cabinet by Boston maker George Croome from the mid-1870s, with a carved crest, columns and a single center door with a bronze medallion.
description: Renaissance Revival furniture was the formal style of choice in American parlors after the Civil War. Croome's cabinet uses its typical elements: a broken crest, columns framing the door, raised panels outlined with moulding and a bronze medallion as a focal point. Mahogany, rosewood and maple are used for contrast. As a reference for modern work, it shows how a single cabinet door can become a feature with framing pilasters and a central ornament, an approach that works for a bar cabinet or a hall console.
makeItToday: Mahogany frame with CNC-carved crest and pilasters, applied mouldings and a cast or CNC-carved medallion.

title: Adler & Sullivan Terra-Cotta Ornament from the Lindauer House Chimney (1885)
summary: An unglazed terra-cotta ornament from the chimney of the Benjamin Lindauer House in Chicago, designed by Adler & Sullivan in 1885, carved with Louis Sullivan's swirling foliate motifs.
description: Louis Sullivan developed one of the most original ornamental languages in American architecture, combining geometry with curling plant forms. This block, about 14 inches across, came from the chimney of a Chicago house his firm designed in 1885. Its deep relief of overlapping leaves around a central spiral is a good model for a carved corbel, a mantel bracket, or an end block on a range hood. Sullivan's ornament reads well at a distance, which is exactly what a feature bracket needs.

title: Adler & Sullivan Cast-Iron Newel Post from the Morris Selz House (1883)
summary: A flat cast-iron newel ornament from the 1883 Morris Selz House in Chicago, designed by Adler & Sullivan with a tall spiral finial and stylized leaf scrolls.
description: This newel is essentially a flat silhouette with a spiral at the top and leafy scrolls at its base, an early example of the ornamental language Sullivan would refine over his career. Because it is a profile rather than a full sculpture, it is a useful reference for modern makers: the same outline can be cut from thick hardwood or plate steel as a stair newel, a balustrade end, or a decorative bracket. The house was demolished in 1967, and the piece survives in the Art Institute of Chicago.

title: Louis Sullivan Elevator Grille from the Chicago Stock Exchange (1894)
summary: A large elevator enclosure grille designed by Louis Sullivan for the Chicago Stock Exchange in 1894, combining a dense band of ornament with a lighter lattice of vertical bars.
description: Sullivan treated even an elevator screen as an occasion for ornament. The grille pairs a band of interlacing foliate panels at the top with lighter vertical bars and a repeating ornamental frieze below. That combination of an ornamental band over a simpler lattice is exactly the formula a good radiator cover or vent screen needs: enough openness for air to flow, with decoration concentrated where the eye lands. The Chicago Stock Exchange was demolished in 1972; this grille survives at the Art Institute of Chicago.
makeItToday: CNC-pierced hardwood or MDF grille panels set into a painted frame; ensure at least 40 to 50 percent open area for radiator airflow.

summary: A tall cast-iron panel from the Rothschild Store in Chicago, designed by Adler & Sullivan in 1881, with a fan of stylized leaves rising from a central stem.
description: This early Sullivan panel shows his ornament before it became densely interwoven: a symmetrical fan of leaves and buds grows from a central stem inside a simple frame. Its clarity makes it an easy motif to adapt. As a carved door panel, a pilaster face on a mantel, or the end panel of an island, it brings late-Victorian character without heavy period detail. The store was demolished in 1972; the panel is preserved at the Art Institute of Chicago.

title: Thorne Miniature Room: New York Parlor, 1850–70
summary: A 1:12-scale Thorne Room reconstructing a mid-19th-century New York parlor with Rococo Revival furniture, tall windows with layered drapery and a central built-in bookcase.
description: Narcissa Niblack Thorne's miniature rooms, built by Chicago artisans in the 1930s and 1940s, are among the clearest visual histories of American interiors. This parlor represents a prosperous New York home of the 1850s and 1860s: tall windows with heavy drapery, a carved center bookcase built into the wall, gilded cornices, and Rococo Revival seating. The architectural trim is broad and layered. For anyone restoring or recreating a mid-Victorian room, it is a useful guide to the scale of door casings, cornices and built-in cases.

summary: A 1:12-scale Thorne Room of a typical American parlor of the 1870s and 1880s, with a painted mantel, patterned wallpaper, a tall secretary and mixed Victorian furnishings.
description: This Thorne Room represents an ordinary middle-class parlor rather than a mansion, which makes it especially useful for owners of modest Victorian homes. The fireplace has a simple painted mantel with an overmantel mirror, the trim is moderate in scale, and furniture of several revival styles shares the room. It shows how Victorian rooms were actually lived in: layered, eclectic and personal. A mantel of this type is one of the most achievable period upgrades for an older house.

summary: The front parlor of the Molly Brown House Museum in Denver, a Queen Anne-style home completed in 1889, furnished and restored to its late-Victorian appearance.
description: The Molly Brown House on Pennsylvania Street in Denver's Capitol Hill was home to Margaret Brown, remembered as a survivor of the Titanic. Its restored parlor is one of the best places in Colorado to see late-Victorian interior woodwork in place: carved mantels, layered door and window casings, and furniture of the period. Carol M. For Colorado owners of Victorian houses in Capitol Hill, Curtis Park or the mountain mining towns, it is a local reference for the scale and finish of original trim.

title: American Marble Mantelpiece with Carved Arched Opening (c. 1853)
summary: A white marble mantelpiece made in America around 1853, with an arched firebox opening, a carved central cartouche and a deep shelf, typical of mid-19th-century city parlors.
description: Arched marble mantels like this one filled the front parlors of American townhouses in the 1850s. The design is restrained: a softly arched opening, a carved cartouche at the keystone, scrolled shoulders and a deep, moulded shelf. Their proportions translate well to wood. A paint-grade or stained-hardwood version, with the arch and cartouche carved on the CNC, can bring the same character to a fireplace that has lost its original surround. The Metropolitan Museum's example is roughly 50 by 74 inches, a useful benchmark for scale.

title: Dining Room Built-ins, Molly Brown House, Denver
summary: The dining room of the Molly Brown House Museum in Denver, showing a built-in mirrored sideboard and a glazed china cabinet set into the room's late-Victorian woodwork.
description: Victorian dining rooms were designed around storage for china, silver and linens. In the Molly Brown House, completed in 1889, a mirrored sideboard and a glazed china cabinet are integrated with the room's woodwork, and a bay of tall windows brings in light. The museum displays period clothing in the room, as seen here. Built-in dining storage is one of the most practical features to recreate in an older Denver home, and it works equally well as a coffee bar or butler's pantry today.

summary: A decorated interior doorknob and rosette in the Molly Brown House Museum in Denver, typical of the cast, patterned hardware used in high-style houses of the 1880s.

Details like this set the scale for everything around them: a richly patterned knob looks right against a substantial casing and a paneled door. Metal hardware is not part of our custom woodwork range, but this entry is in the reference library because hardware is the first thing to plan when a period door or cabinet is made. title: Thorne Miniature Room: Massachusetts Drawing Room, 1768
summary: A 1:12-scale Thorne Room of a Massachusetts drawing room of 1768, with painted raised-panel walls, pilasters and a classical chimneypiece typical of prosperous New England houses before the Revolution.
description: Colonial New England drawing rooms were often fully paneled on the fireplace wall, with the rest of the room finished with a paneled dado and plaster above. This miniature captures that hierarchy: the chimney breast is framed by fluted pilasters and topped with a classical entablature, while the side walls are simpler. The paint color unifies everything. It is a useful model for anyone adding a paneled fireplace wall to a Colonial Revival house, because it shows how much detail to give the focal wall and how quiet to keep the rest.

Paint, rather than stain, was common in rural Pennsylvania and remains a forgiving finish today.

Most of the ornament here is plaster, but the same framing system can be achieved in wood with applied mouldings, which is how many Colonial Revival houses interpreted it.

Its design language, of carved frieze rails, geometric panels and bulbous turnings, is the basis of much Tudor Revival cabinetry. summary: The drawing room of Red House in Bexleyheath, the home Philip Webb designed for William Morris in 1859–60, with its painted built-in settle and cupboard and open timber details.

A painted built-in settle or window seat with a cupboard above is still one of the most characterful additions to a living room or reading nook.

title: Library Bookcases, Clare College, Cambridge (measured drawing, 1903)
summary: A measured drawing from Tanner's English Interior Woodwork of early 17th-century library bookcases at Clare College, Cambridge, with carved cresting and panelled ends.
description: College libraries in Oxford and Cambridge preserve some of the earliest English built-in bookcases. The Clare College cases, from about the 1620s according to Tanner, have panelled ends, shelves between them and decorative cresting on top. They are a direct ancestor of the built-in library. For a modern study, the panelled-end case with a carved top is a handsome way to give built-in shelving a Jacobean character.

title: Shaker Built-In Cupboard (Index of American Design, 1937)

description: The Index of American Design was a Depression-era project that employed artists to record American decorative arts in precise watercolors. This rendering shows a Shaker cupboard built into the wall next to a doorway, with stacked panelled doors and trim that matches the door casing. It is a clear template for using the space beside a door or in a wall recess for storage that looks original to the house.

title: A. W. N. Pugin Brass Grille from the Palace of Westminster (c. 1845–59)
summary: A pierced brass grille designed by A. W. N. Pugin for the Palace of Westminster in London, with a repeating pattern of Gothic foliage and quatrefoil-like openings.
description: Augustus Pugin designed thousands of fittings for the rebuilt Houses of Parliament, from tiles to door furniture. This small brass grille, about 21 by 14 inches, uses a repeating diagonal lattice of stylized leaves and flowers, with openings large enough for air to pass. It is a ready-made pattern for a radiator cover, a heating register face or a cabinet door insert in a Gothic or Victorian room. Pierced patterns like this are well suited to CNC cutting in wood or metal.

title: Dining Hall at Great Camp Sagamore, Adirondacks
summary: The dining hall at Great Camp Sagamore in New York's Adirondack Mountains, a log-and-timber room with large windows looking out over the lake.
description: Great Camp Sagamore was built in the late 1890s by William West Durant and later owned by the Vanderbilt family. Its buildings are classic Adirondack rustic architecture, with log and timber construction, dark wood interiors and large windows framing the lake. The dining hall's dark wood walls and tall divided windows create a dramatic, cozy space. The Adirondack great camps are an important source for mountain design across the United States.

title: Lobby of El Tovar Hotel, Grand Canyon (historic photograph)
summary: A historic photograph of the lobby of El Tovar Hotel at the Grand Canyon's South Rim, opened in 1905, with a beamed ceiling, rustic furniture and patterned rugs.
description: El Tovar was built by the Santa Fe Railway in 1905 as a grand hotel at the canyon's edge, combining log construction with refined interiors. This historic view shows its lobby with a coffered, beamed ceiling, wicker and wood furniture, and wood-paneled walls. The beamed ceiling is the standout feature, a pattern of timber beams that can be reproduced with box beams in a modern house.
